Situation 24 · “Not Spicy, Please”Culture
Pro-Tip · Season at the Table

Khmer cooking is built to be adjusted by the eater, which is why every table carries chilli, fish sauce, sugar, lime and pepper. Ordering mild and then seasoning your own bowl is completely normal and slightly insults nobody. The famous exception is ទឹកត្រី (tuk-trei, fermented fish sauce) — it is already inside almost every dish, so a genuine fish allergy needs stating clearly and early.

Say it right

ហឹរ (hoeu) is spicy-hot; ក្ដៅ (kdav) is hot in temperature. Asking for food that is not kdav will get you a cold plate.

Situation 25 · Street Food StallsCulture
Pro-Tip · Follow the Queue

The safest stall is the busiest one — high turnover means nothing sits warm for hours. Look for a crowd of Cambodians rather than a sign in English, and eat where the cooking happens in front of you. Som douch koat — “the same as him” — is the single most useful sentence at a stall, and it usually gets you the thing the regulars actually come for.

Say it right

យកទៅផ្ទះ (yok teuv phteah) literally means “take it home” and is how Cambodians say takeaway. Your food arrives in a plastic bag tied with an elastic band.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 26 · Asking for the BillCulture
Pro-Tip · Dollars In, Riel Out

Cambodia runs on two currencies at once. You pay in US dollars and receive change under one dollar in riel, at a fixed rate of about 4,000 riel to the dollar. So a $3.50 bill settled with a $5 note comes back as one dollar and 2,000 riel. Refuse torn or heavily marked dollar notes — shops will refuse them from you later.

Say it right

គិតលុយ (ket luy) literally means “count the money”. Add phong at the end and a raised hand, and it is warm rather than brusque.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 27 · Praising & ComplainingCulture
Pro-Tip · Complain Softly, Get More

Raising your voice in a Cambodian restaurant loses you the argument instantly — the staff will smile, freeze, and quietly stop helping. Public anger causes a loss of face on both sides. Open every complaint with som toh, keep your tone flat and friendly, and you will usually get the dish replaced and something free. The soft approach is not politeness here; it is the effective one.

Say it right

ឆ្ងាញ់ (chhngañ) ends in the ny of canyon, closed off without release. It is the highest praise you can pay a Cambodian cook, and it costs one syllable.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 28 · Vegetarian & AllergiesCulture
Pro-Tip · Name the Ingredient, Not the Diet

Categories travel badly; ingredients do not. “Vegetarian” may still arrive with chicken stock or a spoon of fish sauce, because those are seasonings rather than meat in the local sense. Say instead: no pork, no chicken, no fish, no fish sauce — four short phrases, listed one by one. For a serious allergy, have a Cambodian friend write it in Khmer on a card and show that; it removes every gap in pronunciation.

Say it right

បួស (buoh) carries a Buddhist sense — food fit for a monk on holy days. Saying khnyom nyam buoh is understood immediately, where the English word “vegetarian” often is not.

Situation 29 · Ordering DeliveryCulture
Pro-Tip · Save Your Address in Khmer

Type your address in Khmer script into your phone’s notes once, with the nearest landmark, and paste it into every delivery order afterwards. Riders navigate by landmark plus phone call, not by GPS pin — pins in Phnom Penh are frequently thirty metres and one alley wrong. Adding nov choab … (“next to …”) to the order note saves the call altogether.

Say it right

ជាប់ (choab) means “attached to / right next to”. nov choab … is far more useful to a rider than any street name.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 30 · A Guest at a Khmer MealCulture
Pro-Tip · Let the Eldest Start

Wait for the oldest person at the table to lift their spoon before you touch yours, and serve them before yourself if a dish is near you. Take small portions from the shared bowls onto your own plate rather than eating out of the middle. You will be pressed to eat more long after you are full — khnyom chha-aet haoy with a hand over the bowl is the accepted way to stop, and it may take saying twice.

Say it right

ពិសា (pisaa) is the polite word for to eat, used for guests and elders; ញ៉ាំ (nyam) is the everyday one. Hearing pisaa means you are being honoured.

Situation 31 · At the MarketCulture
Pro-Tip · Find One Seller and Stay

Cambodian markets run on relationships, not on comparison shopping. Buy from the same vegetable seller every week and within a month you will be given the good tomatoes without asking, quoted the local price automatically, and handed free herbs. Learn her name, greet her before you buy, and the market stops being a place you negotiate and becomes a place you are known.

Say it right

Open with bong before the question. Walking up and firing pon-man? at a seller sounds like an interrogation; one warm syllable in front changes the whole exchange.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 32 · BargainingCulture
Pro-Tip · Walking Away Is the Real Offer

Say khnyom ket sen — “let me think about it” — and start walking. If your price was workable you will be called back within five steps; if you are not called back, it genuinely was too low. This is understood as part of the game by both sides. What is not acceptable is bargaining hard and then not buying: settle a price only on something you actually intend to take.

Say it right

The magic word is baan tei? — “is that possible?” Attach it to any number and you have made an offer without ever sounding demanding.

Situation 33 · Asking the PriceCulture
Pro-Tip · Carry Small Notes

Handing a $50 note to a market seller for a $2 purchase will stop the transaction entirely — nobody at street level holds that much change, and you will be sent to break it yourself. Keep ones, fives and riel notes in a separate pocket. In supermarkets and petrol stations, large notes are fine; everywhere else, the small money is what makes you easy to serve.

Say it right

Riel are quoted in thousands and ten-thousands: muoy poan is 1,000 and មួយម៉ឺន (muoy meun) is 10,000. Miss meun and you will hear the price as ten times too little.

Situation 34 · Clothes, Sizes & ColoursCulture
Pro-Tip · Have It Altered

Tailoring is cheap and everywhere. A market shirt that almost fits can be taken in for a dollar or two by the ជាងកាត់ដេរ (chieng kat-dei, tailor) sitting three stalls away — often on the spot. This is why Cambodians buy clothes that are slightly loose rather than slightly tight, and why thom chieng nih bon-tech is the more useful of the two size phrases above.

Say it right

Comparatives use ជាង (chieng) after the adjective: thom chieng nih — “bigger than this”, literally “big more-than this”.

Situation 35 · At the MinimartCulture
Pro-Tip · Check the Date on Dairy

Power cuts are common and the cold chain is not always unbroken, so milk, yoghurt and imported cheese deserve a glance at the date — ផុតកំណត់ (phot kom-not), “expiry”. Minimart prices are fixed and marked, so no bargaining happens here; that is precisely what makes them a comfortable place to practise your Khmer without any money riding on the outcome.

Say it right

មាន … ទេ? (mien … tei?) — “do you have …?” — is the workhorse shopping question. Slot any noun into the middle and you can shop anywhere in the country.

Situation 36 · At the PharmacyCulture
Pro-Tip · Ask for the Box

Cambodian pharmacies often dispense loose tablets in a small plastic bag with the dosage written on it, and antibiotics are sold without a prescription. Ask for the original box so you can read the drug name and strength — som yok bratab phong, “the packet too, please”. If symptoms last more than three days, or involve a high fever, go to a clinic rather than back to the pharmacy: dengue is common and needs a blood test.

Say it right

ឈឺ (chheu) means “to hurt / be sick” and takes the body part straight after it: chheu kbaal (head), chheu poh (stomach), chheu thmenh (tooth).

Situation 37 · Riel & DollarsCulture
Pro-Tip · The 4,000 Rule

The rate is pegged at roughly 4,000 riel to one dollar and barely moves, so the arithmetic is easy: 2,000 riel is fifty cents, 10,000 riel is $2.50. Dollars handle the large amounts, riel handles everything under a dollar — there are no US coins in circulation at all. Torn or ink-marked dollar bills are routinely refused, so inspect the notes you are given before you walk away.

Say it right

លុយតូចៗ (luy touch-touch) — literally “small small money” — is how you ask for small denominations. It is the most practically useful request on this page.

Situation 38 · Bank & ATM ProblemsCulture
Pro-Tip · Withdraw Dollars, Not Riel

Most Cambodian ATMs let you choose the currency. Take dollars — riel withdrawals come out in large notes that small shops cannot break. Machines also charge a flat fee of around $4 to $5 per withdrawal regardless of amount, so take out more, less often. Choose an ATM inside a bank branch during opening hours: if it eats your card at 9 p.m. on a Friday, nobody can open it until Monday.

Say it right

ដក (dok) is “to withdraw” and ដាក់ (dak) is “to deposit / put in”. One vowel apart, opposite meanings — worth drilling before you stand at a counter.

Situation 39 · SIM Cards & Top-UpCulture
Pro-Tip · Buy It in the Shop, Not the Street

SIM registration is legally tied to a passport, and a card sold pre-registered under a stranger’s name can be cut off without warning. Go to a branded Smart, Cellcard or Metfone shop, hand over your passport, and have them register it to you. Data is extremely cheap by international standards — a few dollars buys a generous monthly package — and coverage is good in towns, patchy on rural roads.

Say it right

Topping up is បញ្ចូលទឹកប្រាក់ (banh-choul tuk-brak) — literally “pour in water-money”. Shops with a phone-company sign outside will do it in fifteen seconds.

Situation 40 · Returns & ExchangesCulture
Pro-Tip · Test It Before You Leave

There is no legal right to return goods you simply changed your mind about, and most small shops operate on “sold is sold”. So test everything at the counter: plug in the charger, switch on the fan, check both shoes, unfold the whole garment. Electronics from proper stores carry a genuine ធានា (thie-nie, guarantee) — keep that slip somewhere safe, because without it repairs are charged in full.

Say it right

ប្ដូរ (bdo) is “to exchange”; សងលុយវិញ (song luy vinh) is “to give the money back”. Ask for the first — the second rarely exists here.

Situation 41 · Checking InCulture
Pro-Tip · Always Ask to See It

Inspecting the room before agreeing is completely normal and nobody is offended by it — guesthouses expect it. Check three things: that the air conditioning actually blows cold, that hot water reaches the shower, and that the window does not open onto a karaoke bar. Rooms on the same floor at the same price often differ enormously, and asking to see a second one usually gets you the better of the two.

Say it right

សិន (sen) at the end of a request means “first, before anything else”. som meul … sen is the polite way to inspect before committing.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 42 · Hotel Requests & ProblemsCulture
Pro-Tip · Report It the Same Day

Saying nothing and then complaining at checkout gets you nowhere; reporting a fault immediately almost always gets it fixed or gets you moved. Keep the tone light — a problem raised with a smile is a favour asked, and a favour asked is a favour granted. Power cuts are frequent in the provinces, so a guesthouse with a ម៉ាស៊ីនភ្លើង (maa-sin phleung, generator) is worth a dollar or two more per night.

Say it right

គ្មាន … ទេ (kmien … tei) means “there isn’t any …”. It is the negative twin of mien … tei? and reports a missing thing without blaming anybody.

Situation 43 · Checking OutCulture
Pro-Tip · Luggage Storage Is Free

Nearly every guesthouse will hold your bag for the day after checkout at no charge, which turns an awkward afternoon before a night bus into a free one. Ask with phnhaeu kaa-boub tuk baan tei? and take anything valuable with you. Tipping is not expected in Cambodian hotels, but leaving a couple of dollars for the cleaner is quietly appreciated and very unusual.

Say it right

ផ្ញើ (phnhaeu) means “to entrust / leave in someone’s care” — used for luggage, parcels and money alike. It implies you will come back for it.

Situation 44 · Apartment HuntingCulture
Pro-Tip · The Electricity Rate Is the Real Rent

Landlords in Cambodia commonly resell electricity at well above the state rate, and with air conditioning running you can add a hundred dollars a month without noticing. Always ask the price per unit and compare it against the official EDC tariff before signing. Two months’ deposit is standard, and getting it back at the end depends almost entirely on the relationship you build — so photograph the whole flat on the day you move in.

Say it right

មិនរាប់ (min roab) means “not counting / not including”. When a landlord says it about phleung tuk, ask the unit rate immediately.

Situation 45 · Talking to the LandlordCulture
Pro-Tip · Give a Month’s Notice, in Person

Contracts here are often short and informally enforced, so what protects you is goodwill rather than paperwork. Announce a departure a full month ahead and face to face, never by message, and pay the last month rather than asking to have it taken from the deposit — that single gesture is what usually gets the deposit returned. A small gift at Khmer New Year does more for your tenancy than any clause.

Say it right

Call your landlord bong if they are near your age, om if they are your parents’ generation. Getting this right shapes the entire relationship — and the relationship is what gets things repaired.

Situation 46 · Electricity, Water & Wi-FiCulture
Pro-Tip · Photograph the Meter

Take a picture of the electricity meter on the day you move in and on the first of every month. It costs ten seconds and settles every billing dispute instantly, because you can show the reading rather than argue about it. Keep a torch and a power bank charged: cuts of two or three hours are ordinary, especially in the hot season when the whole city runs its air conditioning at once.

Say it right

ដាច់ (dach) means “cut off” and applies to power, water, internet and roads alike: dach phleung, dach tuk, dach phlov.

Situation 47 · Calling a RepairmanCulture
Pro-Tip · Agree the Price Before He Opens It

Once a machine is in pieces on your floor your negotiating position has gone. Ask chuoh-chul oh pon-man? at the door, and ask again if he discovers a second fault. Most repairmen are found by asking your neighbours rather than searching online — the one who fixed the flat downstairs will come faster, charge the local rate and care about his reputation on your street.

Say it right

ខូច (khouch) covers every kind of broken — machines, phones, roads, even food that has gone off. Point at the thing and say it; you will be understood.

Situation 48 · Hiring a CleanerCulture
Pro-Tip · Pay Well and Pay on Time

Domestic work is often the household’s main income, and a day’s pay missed matters. Agree the rate openly at the start, pay on the day you promised, and add a month’s wage as a bonus at Khmer New Year — this is expected of good employers, not optional generosity. Praise directly and correct gently; criticism given in front of anyone else causes real loss of face and is rarely recovered from.

Say it right

Days of the week all begin with ថ្ងៃ (thngai): thngai chan Monday, thngai ong-kie Tuesday, thngai sok Friday, thngai aa-tit Sunday.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai
Situation 49 · Neighbours & SecurityCulture
Pro-Tip · Your Street Is Your Security System

Introduce yourself to the neighbours and the chhmam in your first week, and greet them every single day afterwards. On a Cambodian street, people watch out for those they know by name — the guard who has been handed a cold drink on a hot afternoon will notice a stranger at your gate. Weddings and funerals on the street are loud and go on for days; complaining about them marks you out, while attending for ten minutes makes you a neighbour.

Say it right

សូមស្វាគមន៍ (som svie-kom) is “welcome”. You will hear it constantly — at doors, at shops, and on every hotel sign in the country.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 50 · LaundryCulture
Pro-Tip · Count It In and Count It Out

Laundry shops wash several households together, so socks and single shirts do migrate. Count the items as you hand them over — the staff will happily count with you, and it is entirely normal — then count them again on collection. In the rainy season, clothes may come back not quite dry and smelling of it; a shop with a proper ម៉ាស៊ីនសម្ងួត (maa-sin som-nguot, dryer) is worth walking an extra street for.

Say it right

បោកគក់ (baok-kok) is the everyday word for doing laundry. Shops advertise it on hand-painted signs alongside the price per kilo.

Situation 51 · Describing SymptomsCulture
Pro-Tip · Fever Plus Aches Means a Blood Test

Dengue is common across Cambodia and its early signs look exactly like flu: high fever, headache behind the eyes, deep muscle ache. If a fever lasts more than two days, go to a clinic and ask for a blood test rather than taking more paracetamol — and avoid ibuprofen or aspirin, which are dangerous in dengue. Say khnyom chong pinet chhiem: “I want a blood test.”

Say it right

ក្ដៅខ្លួន (kdav kluon) is literally “hot body” — a fever. Do not say khnyom kdav alone; that just means you are feeling warm.

Situation 52 · At the DoctorCulture
Pro-Tip · Know Your Nearest Good Clinic Now

Find out today — before you need it — which clinic in your town handles foreigners, and save the number. In Phnom Penh and Siem Reap there are international clinics with English-speaking doctors; in the provinces, standards vary a great deal and serious cases are often evacuated to the capital or to Bangkok. If you are staying long term, medical insurance that covers evacuation is the single most valuable thing you can buy.

Say it right

គ្រូពេទ្យ (kruu-peit) is a doctor; មន្ទីរពេទ្យ (mon-ti-peit) is a hospital. Both contain peit, the root for medicine.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 53 · At the DentistCulture
Pro-Tip · Dental Work Is a Bargain

Cambodia has a large number of well-trained dentists, many educated abroad, and prices are a fraction of Western ones — a cleaning costs a few dollars, a filling perhaps twenty. Foreigners living here often schedule dental work deliberately during their stay. Choose a clinic that shows you sterile packaging opened in front of you, and ask what the total will be before treatment starts, not after.

Say it right

ធ្មេញ (thmenh) begins with a puffed t pressed straight into m — one syllable, no vowel between. Say “t-menh”, not “ta-menh”.

Situation 54 · Medicine & DosageCulture
Pro-Tip · Finish the Antibiotics

Antibiotics are sold freely here and are often handed out for ordinary colds, which they do nothing for. If you are genuinely prescribed a course, finish all of it even once you feel well — stopping early is how resistant infections are bred, and Southeast Asia already has a serious problem with them. Also check every packet’s expiry date at the counter: stock rotation in small pharmacies is not always careful.

Say it right

Repeat instructions back with … maen tei? — “correct?”. It turns a one-way instruction into a confirmed one, and pharmacists appreciate it.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 55 · Calling for HelpCulture
Pro-Tip · Get to the Hospital Yourself

Ambulance coverage is limited and slow outside the capital, and in a real emergency Cambodians drive the patient in themselves — by car, by tuk-tuk, by motorbike. Do the same rather than waiting. Keep three things written in Khmer in your wallet or phone: your blood type, any allergy, and the name of the nearest hospital. The national emergency numbers are 119 for ambulance, 117 for police and 118 for fire.

Say it right

ជួយផង! (chuoy phong!) is the shout for help. Two syllables, loud, repeated — this is the one phrase in the book to memorise before you need to look it up.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 56 · Reporting a TheftCulture
Pro-Tip · Bag Snatching From Motorbikes

The commonest crime against foreigners in Phnom Penh is a bag pulled from a passing motorbike, which can drag you into the road. Carry bags on the side away from traffic, or across your body under an arm, and never hold a phone loosely at the kerb. If it happens, let go — a bag is replaceable. Report it the same day; the station will write a report, sometimes for a small unofficial fee, and insurers require it.

Say it right

លួច (luoch) is “to steal” and បាត់ (bat) is “to be lost”. Choose carefully: one is a crime report, the other is a lost-property enquiry.

Situation 57 · A Traffic AccidentCulture
Pro-Tip · Fault Follows the Larger Vehicle

In practice, responsibility here is often assigned to whoever was driving the bigger vehicle — and to the foreigner, who is assumed able to pay. Disputes are usually settled on the spot with cash rather than through insurers. Stay calm, never raise your voice, photograph everything including both number plates, and phone a Khmer-speaking friend to negotiate for you. Above all, do not drive away: leaving the scene turns a claim into a criminal matter.

Say it right

Ask neak ro-buoh tei? — “are you injured?” — before anything else. Beginning with concern rather than blame changes how the entire situation unfolds.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 58 · Massage & SpaCulture
Pro-Tip · Look for the Blind Massage Centres

Cambodia has a network of training centres employing blind and partially sighted therapists, and the standard of traditional Khmer massage there is generally excellent — firm, technical, and priced at a few dollars an hour. Seeing Hands is the best known. A tip of a dollar or two is genuinely appreciated. Note that Khmer massage involves stretching and deep pressure rather than oil and gliding; thnom-thnom is not a sign of weakness, it is useful information.

Say it right

ថ្នមៗ (thnom-thnom) means “gently, softly”, and ខ្លាំង (khlang) means “strong”. Between them you can steer any massage in the country.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 59 · At the GymCulture
Pro-Tip · Exercise at Dawn or Dusk

Cambodians train early and late, never in the middle of the day — by ten in the morning the heat makes outdoor exercise genuinely risky. Head to any riverside or public park at around six in the evening and you will find free open-air aerobics classes, dozens of people following an instructor with a speaker, for a few hundred riel or nothing at all. It is the friendliest possible way to practise both your fitness and your Khmer.

Say it right

ហាត់ប្រាណ (hat bran) means “to exercise”. A gym is កន្លែងហាត់ប្រាណ (kon-laeng hat bran) — literally “the exercising place”.

Situation 60 · Stress, Sleep & Feeling LowCulture
Pro-Tip · Feelings Live in the Heart Word

A great many Khmer emotional expressions are built on ចិត្ត (chet), meaning heart or mind: sa-bay chet is happy, min sa-bay chet unhappy, khoeung chet angry, smoh chet sincere. Mental health is rarely discussed openly here and there are few local services, so long-term residents often rely on international clinics in Phnom Penh or on counselling online. Saying you are simply hot — tired — is always understood, and always an acceptable answer.

Say it right

នឹករលឹក (neuk ro-leuk) means “to miss / long for”. Say khnyom neuk ro-leuk phteah and any Cambodian will understand exactly what you mean.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 61 · Job Interview BasicsCulture
Pro-Tip · Modesty Reads Better Than Confidence

Western interview style — listing achievements, selling yourself hard — can land badly here, where self-promotion is read as a lack of humility. Cambodian candidates tend to describe what the team accomplished and what they still hope to learn. If you are the one interviewing, note that a quiet candidate is not necessarily an unconfident one; ask what they did rather than how good they are, and you will get a far more accurate answer.

Say it right

ណែនាំខ្លួន (nae-noam kluon) means “introduce oneself”. The same verb nae-noam is used for recommending a person or a restaurant.

Situation 62 · Professional IntroductionsCulture
Pro-Tip · Greet the Most Senior Person First

Cambodian offices are strongly hierarchical, and the order in which you greet a room is noticed by everyone in it. Identify the most senior person — usually the oldest, and the one others defer to — and greet them first, with a sampeah slightly higher than you would use for peers. Use lowk or lowk srei until you are invited to do otherwise, and let them set the tone for how formal the meeting stays.

Say it right

Give and receive a card with both hands, or with the right hand supported at the elbow by the left. Read it before putting it away — never straight into a back pocket.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 63 · In a MeetingCulture
Pro-Tip · Silence Is Not Agreement

Juniors rarely contradict seniors in front of a room, so a meeting that ends with everyone nodding may have settled nothing at all. The real conversation happens afterwards, one to one. If you are leading, ask people individually and privately, and always finish by asking each person to state back what they will do and by when. Written follow-up in Khmer or simple English prevents the polite nod from becoming a missed deadline.

Say it right

ប្រហែល (bra-hael, “perhaps”) is how Cambodians disagree. “Perhaps there is another way” is a full objection — treat it as one.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 64 · Work Phone CallsCulture
Pro-Tip · Business Runs on Telegram

Cambodia does most of its professional messaging on Telegram rather than email — quotes, invoices, contracts and appointments all arrive there, often as photographs of paper documents. Expect voice notes rather than typed replies, and expect to be added to a great many groups. Email is treated as formal and slow; if something is urgent, phone. And answer with your company name, as above: it is what callers expect to hear.

Say it right

គាត់ (koat) is the respectful third-person pronoun for an adult — “he” or “she” alike. Khmer pronouns mark status, not gender.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 65 · Messages & AppointmentsCulture
Pro-Tip · Confirm the Morning Of

An appointment agreed a week ahead is an intention, not a commitment; traffic, rain, family obligations and more senior people all outrank it. Send a short confirming message on the morning of the meeting — this is normal practice, not nagging, and it is how Cambodians manage their own diaries. Build slack into your day, and treat a cancellation as circumstance rather than rudeness.

Say it right

ណាត់ជួប (nat chuop) means “to make an appointment”. បញ្ជាក់ (banh-cheak) means “to confirm” — always do the second after the first.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 66 · Small Talk at WorkCulture
Pro-Tip · Eat Lunch With the Team

Lunch in a Cambodian office is a shared, communal affair, often eaten together at someone’s desk or at the same stall every day. Turning it down repeatedly to work through — a virtue in some workplaces — reads here as keeping yourself apart. Say yes, pay your share, ask about people’s families and home provinces, and the working relationship that follows will be far more open than any number of meetings could produce.

Say it right

ស្រុកកំណើត (srok kom-naeut) is “home village / birthplace”. Almost everyone working in Phnom Penh has one, and asking about it is a warm, safe question.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 67 · Instructing StaffCulture
Pro-Tip · Correct in Private, Praise in Public

Criticising someone in front of colleagues causes a loss of face that can quietly end their willingness to work with you, and they will rarely tell you so. Correct quietly, one to one, and soften it — khoh bon-tech, “slightly wrong”, does the job. Praise, by contrast, should be given openly. And never ask yul tei? expecting a truthful no; ask instead for the task to be explained back to you.

Say it right

Frame instructions as requests: chuoy … phong means “please help … ”. A bare command is grammatically fine and socially cold; the chuoy … phong wrapper costs two words.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

To signចុះហត្ថលេខាchoh hat-tha-lei-khaa
Is there a guarantee?មានធានាទេ?mien thie-nie tei?
Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai
Situation 68 · Negotiating a ContractCulture
Pro-Tip · Bilingual, and Two Copies

Have any contract that matters drawn up in Khmer and English side by side, with both parties signing every page and each keeping an original. Where the two versions differ, the Khmer text is what a Cambodian court will read — so pay a local lawyer to check it rather than relying on a translation you cannot verify. Stage the payments against delivered work; a deposit of thirty per cent is normal, paying everything up front is not.

Say it right

រួមទាំង (ruom teang) means “including”; មិនរាប់ (min roab) means “not including”. Ask which applies to every line of a quotation.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 69 · In the Language ClassCulture
Pro-Tip · Learn the Alphabet Early

Romanisation gets you speaking in week one — that is what this book is for — but it will quietly cap your progress, because no two systems agree and none captures Khmer vowels exactly. The script has 33 consonants and two vowel series, and most learners can read simple signs after a few weeks of steady work. Start with the consonants you meet daily on shopfronts, and treat every ផ្សារ and វត្ត you pass as a free flashcard.

Say it right

Address a male teacher as លោកគ្រូ (lowk kruu) and a female one as អ្នកគ្រូ (neak kruu). Teachers are held in genuinely high regard in Cambodia.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 70 · Talking About Your JobCulture
Pro-Tip · The Salary Question Is Not Rude

Asking what you earn, what your rent is or what your motorbike cost is ordinary friendly curiosity here, not an intrusion — Cambodians ask each other the same things freely. You are not obliged to answer with a number, and krop-kroan haoy handles it gracefully. Bear in mind that a foreign salary is often many times a local one, so a precise figure can quietly change a friendship; vagueness is kinder to everybody.

Say it right

គ្រប់គ្រាន់ហើយ (krop-kroan haoy) — “it’s enough” — is the perfect answer to a salary question. It is honest, modest, and closes the subject warmly.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 71 · Making PlansCulture
Pro-Tip · Plans Breathe

A Cambodian “yes” to a social plan means yes, in principle. Rain, a family obligation or a request from someone senior will move it without much ceremony, and this is not considered flaky — the relationship matters more than the calendar. Confirm on the day, arrive expecting a flexible start, and do the same yourself without guilt. Friendships here are maintained by frequent small contact rather than by punctual appointments.

Say it right

ទំនេរ (tum-nei) means “free / unoccupied” and works for people, tables and taxis alike. tum-nei tei? is a complete question on its own.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 72 · Inviting Someone OutCulture
Pro-Tip · The Inviter Pays

Splitting a bill item by item is uncommon here. Whoever proposed the outing generally settles it, and the balance is restored next time rather than on the night — which is exactly what leuk kraoy neak means. Bear in mind the income gap: insisting a Cambodian friend on a local salary pay half of a foreigner-priced dinner puts them in a difficult position they will never mention. Pay, lightly, and let them host you somewhere of their choosing later.

Say it right

អញ្ជើញ (an-choeun) is both “to invite” and “please, go ahead”. Whoever says khnyom an-choeun is usually understood to be paying.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 73 · Parties & WeddingsCulture
Pro-Tip · Money in an Envelope

Cambodian weddings are enormous — several hundred guests are ordinary — and the gift is cash in the envelope that came with your invitation, handed in at a table by the door where it is recorded in a book. Twenty to fifty dollars is a normal range depending on how close you are. Dress smartly and brightly; black alone is for funerals. Arriving an hour after the printed time is completely standard, and you may find the party still filling up.

Say it right

អបអរសាទរ (ap-or-saa-to) is “congratulations”, used for weddings, graduations and new babies alike. Four syllables, evenly stressed.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 74 · ComplimentsCulture
Pro-Tip · Deflect, Don’t Accept

Receiving praise with a straight “thank you” can sound like agreement, and agreement sounds like pride. Cambodians deflect first — ot tei, “not at all” — and then thank. Do the same when your Khmer is complimented, which will happen constantly and often generously. Keep compliments to appearance, clothes, home and cooking; comments on a person’s body or weight, normal between close Cambodian friends, are best avoided by a newcomer.

Say it right

ស្អាត (s-at) means both “beautiful” and “clean”. Said of a house it is high praise; said of a person it means good-looking.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 75 · Talking About FamilyCulture
Pro-Tip · The Family Is the Unit

Cambodian identity is rooted in family far more than in the individual, and much of a young worker’s salary goes home to parents in the province every month. Asking after someone’s parents and children is the warmest thing you can do; describing your own family — even briefly, even in poor Khmer — moves you from foreigner to person. If you are over thirty and unmarried, expect kind bewilderment and possibly an introduction.

Say it right

បងប្អូន (bong-p’oun) literally means “elder-younger” and covers all siblings at once. Khmer marks relative age before it marks gender.

Situation 76 · Visiting Someone’s HomeCulture
Pro-Tip · Shoes Off, Head Down, Feet Away

Three rules cover most of home etiquette. Take your shoes off at the door, always. Lower your head slightly when passing in front of someone seated and older. And never point the soles of your feet at a person or at the household shrine — sit cross-legged or with your feet tucked behind you. The head is the most sacred part of the body and the feet the least, which is why patting even a child’s head is best avoided.

Say it right

កក់ក្ដៅ (kok-kdav) literally means “warm”, but of a home it means welcoming and full of affection — a compliment any host is pleased to hear.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 77 · Giving & Receiving GiftsCulture
Pro-Tip · Give With Two Hands, Don’t Expect It Opened

Offer and receive gifts with both hands, and do not be surprised when yours is set aside unopened — opening a present in front of the giver can seem greedy, so it is enjoyed privately later. Fruit, cakes and useful household things travel well; avoid anything sharp, and avoid white wrapping or white flowers, which belong to funerals. When visiting a family home, a bag of fruit for the household is always the right answer.

Say it right

ជូន (choun) is the polite verb “to give” — used upwards, to elders and guests. The plain verb ឲ្យ (aoy) is for everyday giving.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 78 · Apologising ProperlyCulture
Pro-Tip · Anger Costs More Than the Problem

Losing your temper in public is remembered long after whatever caused it is forgotten, and it can permanently damage a working or personal relationship. A person who has been shouted at will usually keep smiling — and quietly withdraw. Apologise early, apologise simply, and do not pile on explanations, which read as excuses. A calm kom-hoh khnyom and a small gift the next day repairs almost anything.

Say it right

សូមអភ័យទោស (som a-phey toh) is the full, formal apology; សូមទោស (som toh) is the everyday one. Use the long form when it genuinely matters.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 79 · Saying No PolitelyCulture
Pro-Tip · The Smile-and-Keep-Walking

With persistent street sellers, the effective response is not a firmer no but a softer one delivered while still moving: a smile, ot tei, or-kun, and a small wave without breaking stride. Stopping to explain invites a longer negotiation. Note too that Cambodians rarely refuse outright, so if you hear bra-hael or cham meul sen — “let me see” — from someone, that is very often a polite no.

Say it right

Soften every refusal with or-kun in front and an offer of leuk kraoy — “next time” — behind. A bare ot tei is not wrong, just cold.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 80 · Keeping in TouchCulture
Pro-Tip · Telegram Is the Address Book

Phone numbers here are held on Telegram rather than in email or on paper, and it is where friends, landlords, drivers, colleagues and shops all reach you. Expect voice messages instead of typed ones — recording a reply is faster than typing Khmer script, and it is excellent listening practice for you. Sending chom-riep suor kruo-saa chum-nuoh khnyom, “say hello to your family for me”, is a small courtesy that lands very warmly.

Say it right

ទាក់ទង (teak-tong) means “to contact / be in touch”. teak-tong mok baan krop peil is the standard warm sign-off.

Situation 81 · Angkor & Temple TicketsCulture
Pro-Tip · Cover Your Shoulders and Knees

Angkor is a working sacred site, not only a ruin, and the dress code is enforced at the upper level of Angkor Wat: shoulders and knees covered for everyone. Carry a scarf. Go at sunrise for Angkor Wat and late afternoon for Ta Prohm and Bayon, avoiding the coach hours in between. Children selling postcards at the gates should be politely declined — buying encourages families to keep them out of school.

Say it right

ប្រាសាទ (bra-saat) is a stone temple of the Angkor kind. A living Buddhist monastery is a វត្ត (voat) — a different word entirely.

Situation 82 · Hiring a GuideCulture
Pro-Tip · Ask to See the Licence

Official Angkor guides carry a photo licence badge and have passed real examinations in history and languages; unlicensed guides are cheaper and often far less informed. Book through your guesthouse or the tourism office. A tip of five to ten dollars at the end of a full day is normal and genuinely appreciated, and a guide who has been treated well will happily take you to the quieter temples nobody else visits.

Say it right

មគ្គុទេសក៍ (mok-ku-teih) is a formal word — you will see it on licence badges. In speech many people simply say guide.

Situation 83 · At the PagodaCulture
Pro-Tip · Women Do Not Touch Monks

A monk may not be touched by a woman, nor accept anything directly from her hand — objects are set down on a cloth for him to pick up. This is not a slight; it is monastic discipline, and Cambodian women observe it automatically. Everyone should sit lower than a monk, keep their feet pointed away, and dress with shoulders and knees covered. A donation box at the door is the right place for money.

Say it right

ព្រះ (preah) marks anything sacred — the Buddha, monks, kings. ព្រះសង្ឃ (preah song) is a monk, and the word is always said with care.

Situation 84 · Holidays & FestivalsCulture
Pro-Tip · Plan Around the Big Three

Khmer New Year in mid-April empties the cities entirely as everyone returns to their home village; expect water thrown in the streets and almost nothing open for a week. Pchum Ben in September or October is for feeding the ancestors at the pagoda, and is quieter and more solemn. Bon Om Touk in November fills Phnom Penh’s riverside with boat races and enormous crowds. Book transport weeks ahead, or do not travel at all.

Say it right

បុណ្យ (bon) means both “festival” and “merit”. thveu bon — “to make merit” — is what the festivals are for.

Situation 85 · At the BeachCulture
Pro-Tip · Cambodians Swim Dressed

On local beaches you will notice Cambodian women swimming fully clothed — shirt, shorts, sometimes a hat. Bikinis are normal on tourist beaches at Otres or on the islands, and quietly out of place at a family beach in Kep or Kampot. Sun and sea are stronger than they look; the sun is directly overhead at midday and the currents around the islands are real. Ask hael tuk baan tei? before going in.

Say it right

ហែលទឹក (hael tuk) is “to swim”, literally “swim water”. The sea is សមុទ្រ (sa-mot); a river is ទន្លេ (ton-lei).

Situation 86 · Countryside & VillagesCulture
Pro-Tip · Accept the Coconut

Rural hospitality is offered immediately and generously, often by people with very little, and refusing it politely still reads as refusal. Accept the drink or the fruit, sit down for ten minutes, and answer the questions about where you are from — that is the exchange. Never photograph inside a house or of children without asking. And in remote areas near the Thai border, stay on marked paths: unexploded ordnance is still a genuine hazard.

Say it right

ស្រែ (srae) is a rice field; ស្រូវ (srov) is rice growing in it; បាយ (bay) is cooked rice on your plate. Three words, one crop.

Please don’t photograph.សូមកុំថតsom kom thot
I’ll send you the picture.ខ្ញុំនឹងផ្ញើរូបទៅឲ្យkhnyom neung phnhaeu ruup teuv aoy
Smile!ញញឹម!nho-nheum!
One more, please.សុំមួយទៀតsom muoy tiet
Beautiful photo!រូបស្អាតណាស់!ruup s-at nas!
Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai
Situation 87 · Asking to Take PhotosCulture
Pro-Tip · Ask, Then Actually Send It

Asking first is the difference between a tourist and a guest, and the answer is nearly always a delighted yes. Then keep the promise: take the person’s Telegram number and send the photograph. Many Cambodians have few good pictures of themselves, and a printed copy delivered on a second visit is a gift people remember for years. Never photograph monks without permission, nor children without a parent’s.

Say it right

ថតរូប (thot ruup) is “to take a photo”. Add chie-muoy knie — “together” — and you have asked for a picture with someone rather than of them.

Situation 88 · Cinema & KaraokeCulture
Pro-Tip · Sing Badly, Sing Anyway

Karaoke in Cambodia is done in private rooms with friends and family rather than in front of a bar, and the point is participation, not talent. Refusing the microphone repeatedly is the only real mistake — sing one song, badly, and you will have made a dozen friends. Note that some venues advertised as “KTV” are hostess bars rather than family karaoke; if you are unsure, go where colleagues take you.

Say it right

ច្រៀង (chrieng) is “to sing” and ពីរោះ (pi-roh) is “melodious”. The same word praises a singer and a foreigner’s Khmer.

Situation 89 · Sport & FootballCulture
Pro-Tip · Kun Khmer, Not Muay Thai

Cambodia’s traditional kickboxing is គុនខ្មែរ (kun khmae), broadcast live on Sunday afternoons and followed passionately. Calling it Muay Thai will get you a firm correction — the question of which country originated the sport is a genuinely sensitive one. Football is the other national obsession, and an evening watching the Cambodian national team in a riverside café is one of the easiest ways into ordinary conversation.

Say it right

គាំទ្រ (koam-tro) means “to support”, of a team or a person. ឈ្នះ (chhneah) is win; ចាញ់ (chanh) is lose.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai
Situation 90 · Speaking of HistoryCulture
Pro-Tip · Let Them Raise It First

Almost every Cambodian family lost people under the Khmer Rouge, and almost everyone you meet is connected to that loss. It is not a topic to open over lunch out of curiosity. If someone chooses to tell you their family’s story, that is a considerable trust: listen, don’t compare, don’t ask for details, and thank them. Visit Tuol Sleng and Choeung Ek quietly and without photographing yourself there. Cambodians are far more eager to talk about Angkor, about their food and about the future.

Say it right

សោកស្ដាយ (saok-sday) means “to be sorry / to grieve” — sorrow, not apology. It is the right word when someone tells you of a loss.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 91 · Post Office & ParcelsCulture
Pro-Tip · Use a Courier for Anything Valuable

The state post is inexpensive but slow, and parcels are opened for customs inspection as a matter of routine. For documents or anything of value, use an international courier — more expensive, insured, and genuinely trackable. Never post cash. Note that incoming parcels frequently attract a customs charge on collection, and that the address to give senders is the post office box, since street delivery outside the main cities is limited.

Say it right

ផ្ញើ (phnhaeu) covers sending parcels, messages and money alike. តាមដាន (taam-daan) means “to track / follow”.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 92 · Visa ExtensionCulture
Pro-Tip · Get the Right Visa on Arrival

The tourist visa (T) can be extended only once, for a month. The ordinary visa (E) is the one that extends for six months or a year and permits work — and you cannot switch from T to E without leaving the country. Ask for the E class at the airport if there is any chance you will stay. Overstaying is fined per day at the border and quickly becomes expensive; most long-term residents use an agent, which costs a little more and saves the queue entirely.

Say it right

ពន្យារ (pon-yie) means “to extend / postpone” — the same verb for a visa, a deadline and a meeting.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 93 · Barber & Hair SalonCulture
Pro-Tip · Show a Picture

Hair vocabulary is where careful learners still come unstuck, and the consequences last a month. Show a photograph on your phone and use douch ruup nih — “like this picture”. A cut usually includes a hair wash, a head and shoulder massage and sometimes an ear cleaning, all for two or three dollars. If you would rather skip the ear cleaning, min bach tei, or-kun declines it politely.

Say it right

ខ្លី (khlei) is short and វែង (veng) is long. Add peik — “too” — for the word every haircut needs: kom kat khlei peik.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Situation 94 · Talking to ChildrenCulture
Pro-Tip · Don’t Pat the Head

Ruffling a child’s hair is affectionate in the West and quietly wrong here: the head is the most sacred part of the body. A smile, a wave and a question about school are the right warmth. Please also do not hand money or sweets to begging children, however hard that is — it keeps them working the streets instead of at school. If you want to help, give to a school or a registered organisation instead.

Say it right

Call a child ប្អូន (p’oun) — “younger one”. They will call you bong, or om if you are their parents’ age or older.

Situation 95 · Pets & the VetCulture
Pro-Tip · Rabies Is Real Here

Cambodia has one of the world’s highest rates of rabies deaths, and street dogs are everywhere. Do not approach or feed them, and if you are bitten or even scratched, wash the wound with soap for fifteen minutes and get to a clinic the same day — the Institut Pasteur in Phnom Penh provides the vaccine. Pre-exposure vaccination is well worth it for anyone living here, especially cyclists and families with children.

Say it right

ឆ្កែ (chhkae) is dog and ឆ្មា (chhmaa) is cat. Both begin with the breathy chh that also starts chheu, to hurt.

Situation 96 · Traffic, Noise & GrumblesCulture
Pro-Tip · Grumble Sideways, Not Upward

Complaining companionably about heat, traffic and dust is friendly and expected; complaining at a person about their service or their country is not, and lands much harder than you intend. Note the useful national shrug: អត់អីទេ (ot ei tei) — “never mind”. It carries a genuine Buddhist patience with things that cannot be changed, and reaching for it instead of frustration will make your life here considerably easier.

Say it right

ស្ទះ (stoah) means “blocked” — of traffic, a drain or a nose alike. stoah cha-raa-chor is a traffic jam.

Situation 97 · Opinions & DisagreeingCulture
Pro-Tip · Avoid Politics With Strangers

Cambodians discuss food, family, football and money freely, and national politics far more carefully — particularly with a foreigner they have just met. If a political conversation starts, listen and ask questions rather than offering verdicts about a country you are a guest in. The same applies to religion. Aa-srey, “it depends”, and bra-hael, “perhaps”, are perfectly respectable places to leave an opinion.

Say it right

មិនសូវ (min sao) means “not very / not quite” and is the great softener. min sao yul-srop is a firm disagreement wearing good manners.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

EnglishKhmer ScriptRomanized Phonetics
Past marker (before the verb)បានbaan
Happening nowកំពុងkom-pung

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai
Situation 98 · Telling a StoryCulture
Pro-Tip · The Time Word Does the Work

Because verbs never conjugate, Khmer usually drops the tense marker altogether once a time word has been said: msel-minh khnyom teuv … — “yesterday I go” — is complete and natural. Put the time word at the front of the sentence and the rest looks after itself. This is the moment most learners realise Khmer grammar is far kinder than its script suggests.

Say it right

Three markers carry all of Khmer tense: បាន (baan) before a verb for the past, កំពុង (kom-pung) for right now, នឹង (neung) for the future.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai
Situation 99 · Requests & FavoursCulture
Pro-Tip · Favours Are a Ledger, Not a Transaction

Help given here creates a warm, unspoken obligation that runs in both directions and is never settled with cash. If a colleague spends their Saturday helping you deal with a landlord, the way to repay it is to be available when their family needs something — not to hand them money, which turns a friendship into a service. The word for this debt of kindness is គុណ (kun), and it also sits inside or-kun, thank you.

Say it right

The polite request frame is chuoy + verb + phong. សុំរំខានបន្តិច (som rom-khan bon-tech) — “sorry to disturb” — is the perfect opener.

Ngorn Kakteka · prepared by Nat Bunchhai

Pro-Tip · Goodbyes Take an Hour

Leaving a Cambodian gathering is not a single act but a slow circuit: you announce your departure, are pressed to stay, eat a little more, announce it again, and are walked all the way to your motorbike. Allow for it — leaving abruptly is the one discourtesy. And when you do finally go, the blessing you give matters more than the farewell itself. Som aoy mien sok-kha-phiep la-or — may you have good health — is never the wrong thing to say.

Say it right

ជម្រាបលា (chom-riep lie) is the formal farewell, the mirror of chom-riep suor on page one. You have come full circle.

Situation 100 · Farewells & BlessingsPractice

Practice 6 min

1

Chorus drill 2 min

Model every line twice — once at speed, once syllable by syllable. The class repeats together, then in halves, then individually.

2

Pairs, on their feet 3 min

Students run the whole exchange with a partner, then swap roles. Nobody sits down until both have said every line aloud.

3

Cold call 1 min

Press R to hide the English, point at ជម្រាបលា, and ask three students what it means.
